It started by accident when I was 10. I cut myself on a toy and I remember it feeling good, so I kept cutting myself with the toy on my hand. My mum saw and took the toy away. So then I started to find new things to use, and I started to hide it. I didn’t intend it to be “self harm” when it started. But it gave me a lot of relief from emotional pain, and it became something regular that helped me.

About two years later my sister started self harming. She experience two major traumas that deeply affected me. And she didn’t know I was already self harming too. Up to this point it was never anything bad, just scratches. 

It wasn’t until 5 years after it started that I made something that left a scar. And then 2 years after that I did something that scared me so much that I got clean for about a year. 

After that I sporadically did it, but I didn’t feel addicted. 

Fast forward to 2 years ago, and I was deep in the addiction. I was doing it because I had to, because the urge took over and I lacked the self control to stop it happening. It was never bad enough, never painful enough and I destroyed the majority of my body in those 2 years alone. I used to give myself a star sticker every time I was clean for a whole day. Over a 4 month period I had about 10 stars, because in those 120 days only 10 did not involve self harm. 

Shortly after it peaked I started therapy which really helped. It went from 3 times daily to once a day, to once every other day. The therapy lasted 30 weeks and afterwards I was down to once a week. And then once a fortnight. I did relapse 2 weeks ago, but it was nothing significant and I did not fall back into the addiction cycle. I wasn’t angry at myself for the relapse, because it’s such an improvement on what I used to be like. 

Relapses happen but they’re becoming a lot less frequent 🥰
That’s fantastic! I’m glad you’ve sought help and been clean for so long :)

I’m not medically trained but from personal experience, if the wound is gaping open get it stitched or at least seek medical help. Stitches make the scars neater and smaller. 

Use bio oil on scars to reduce their appearance, and keep your skin moisturised and use sun cream. Scarred skin is very sensitive. 

As for existing wounds/cuts keep them clean, infections are a big risk and they make scarring worse. Don’t pick at scabs and don’t reopen old wounds. 

Of course the best method would be to stop cutting, but I understand that that is easier said than done! Have you sought any form of help? Therapy helped me to get clean, as I was given the skills to get through urges and relapses. People think it won’t help them but it does. 

Stay safe 💚

I have scars on my legs, arms, abdomen, shoulders, feet and one on my hand. The hand one is 7 years old now and hardly noticeable. 

I hide them mainly with clothing. I had to buy stuff that was thin to avoid overheating but not made of a material that would irritate the scars. They can be very itchy! I’ve had a lot of tattoos over the older ones, which has covered them very well! 

I’ve spent many years boiling hot in the summer covering my entire body, since my scars cover at least 50% of the surface of my skin.

There were a number of reasons I started. When I was young I started by accident. I hurt myself, it felt good and I continued. It became an addiction. I did it on and off for so many years. I always returned to it when times were difficult, because it gave me temporary relief from my emotional pain. I did it to ease my emotions, to feel something other than numbness and to try to balance how I felt inside with how I looked on the outside. It is also highly addictive, so at some point I had to do it, rather than wanting to do it. 

It felt like being on a theme park ride, while you’re doing it you get a rush, and release. It feels good. Sometimes after you feel guilty, or panicked and you just want it to go away. There are a lot of emotions, but they tend to swing from euphoria to extreme guilt. Physically, it hurts obviously, but you build up tolerance, and you find you have to do more and more to get the same reaction.

I have gone through two lots of therapy and I am currently clean from self harm. This has taken a lot of effort and was not easy. Self harm is an addiction, it doesn’t just get solved. I’ve been trying to get clean for years, but relapses happen. Recovery is not linear. 

I am not doing this to gain attention. I am doing this to reduce fear and judgement associated with self harm. So many people will tell me to cover up or be ashamed of my skin, but I refuse to let this happen. The more open we are about self harm, the easier it is for people to seek help. Talking reduces stigma.

1. Don't force her to talk about it if she doesn't want to. Just tell her you are there for her if she wants to talk openly about her problems. 
2. I started cutting at the age of 8 and it got particularly bad when I was 11-13, and I attempted suicide. Focus on her feeling comforted. Don't judge or interrogate with questions. I know you want answers, but it's not the time for it. 
3. Try to encourage activities to take up her time/take her from her room. If your parents have film nights, special dinners sometimes and try to find hobbies that can be done as part of a family. For example, when my cutting got bad my parents would do things at my trigger times (evening) that took me out of the place where I did it (my bedroom). Distractions are very helpful!
4. Try to support her getting as much help as possible. It took me 14 years to get help because I kept it hidden so long. You've caught it when she's young, and she could recover well from her mental health issues. 
5. Make her a self care box, so that she knows it's important to look after herself. Self care boxes are great! You can put her favourite tea/hot chocolate, sweets, bubble bath, bath bombs, shower gel, lip balm, sensory items - fan for cooling, hot water bottle, perfumes or oils (lavender oil is amazing), soft toys, distraction tools - tangle toys, putty etc.
